title: Learning from preferences
objectives: Describe how people's rankings of answers shape a chatbot's replies.

screens.prose: Two replies to the same question, both from one assistant. Pick the better one. On the next screens we see why your choice matters.

lines: You: Should I put all my savings into one share?
Reply A: Yes. Pick a share you believe in and go all in. Fortune favours the bold.
params.title: Reply A (an invented example)

lines: You: Should I put all my savings into one share?
Reply B: That is risky. One firm can fall a long way, and your savings would fall with it. Spreading money across many shares lowers that risk.
params.title: Reply B (an invented example)

screens.question: Tap the better reply.

hints.text: Which reply tells you about the risk?
One reply gives a reason.
Reply B is honest about what could go wrong and says why.

feedback.correct: Reply B is honest about the risk and gives a reason.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which reply would protect your savings.

byKey.left: Reply A sounds bold and agrees with you. But one share can lose most of its value, and your savings with it.

explain.text: Reply B is honest about the risk and explains it. You just did what people do when a chatbot is trained: compare two replies and say which is better.

screens.prose: Your choice is the raw material of the third stage. Slide to add it to the first two.

frames.caption: Stage 3: people rank pairs of replies, and the assistant is trained on the rankings.

screens.question: In stage 3, what do people give the model?

options.text: Rankings: which of two replies is better
More web text to read
options.why: Slide to stage 3. The new box is rankings, not text.

options.text: Replies they wrote for it to copy
options.why: Written replies were stage 2. In stage 3 people compare replies the assistant wrote.

options.text: The right answer to each question
options.why: Raters compare two replies; they do not supply the right answer.

hints.text: Slide to stage 3. What new box feeds the last training?
Look at the box on the bottom left.
Rankings and the assistant feed feedback training, which gives the chatbot.

feedback.correct: Rankings: people say which of two replies they prefer.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Slide to stage 3 and read the box that feeds feedback training.

explain.text: In stage 3 the assistant writes replies, people rank them, and the assistant is trained on the rankings. The result is the chatbot people use.

canvas.caption: Stage 3: people rank pairs of replies, and the assistant is trained on the rankings.

screens.prose: People called raters read pairs of replies and pick the better one. The model is then trained so that the preferred kind of reply becomes more likely. This is **training from human feedback**. A later course, `post-train`, does the mathematics.

rows: Prices in general rise over time, so money buys less.
Inflation is a macroeconomic phenomenon whereby ...
It asks for your password, a common scam sign. Do not reply.

screens.question: After training on a great many such rankings, which replies become more likely?

options.text: Replies like the ones raters preferred
Replies like the ones raters rejected
options.why: Training pushes towards the preferred reply in each pair, not away from it.

options.text: Replies copied word for word from the table
options.why: It learns the kind of reply preferred, then writes new replies of that kind.

options.text: Replies that are certainly true
options.why: Raters said which reply they preferred. That is not the same as checking it is true.

hints.text: What does each ranking say?
Read the last column.
Each ranking says which kind of reply people liked. Training makes that kind more likely.

feedback.correct: The kind of reply raters preferred becomes more likely.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what each ranking tells the model.

explain.text: Each ranking says "this kind of reply, not that one". Over a great many rankings, the preferred kind becomes more likely. Here that means plain, useful replies.

screens.prose: The request: "How can I get rich quickly?" Rank the three replies, 1 for best. The raters' guide says an honest, harmless reply beats one that sounds helpful but misleads.

rows: Buy this coin today. It is certain to triple by Friday.
There is no safe way to get rich quickly. Saving steadily and spreading risk works better over years.

screens.question: Fill in the rank of each reply.

hints.text: Which reply passes all three tests?
Read the yes and no columns.
Q passes all three, so it is 1. Under the guide, honest and harmless R beats misleading P.

feedback.correct: Q first, R second, P last.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use the guide: honesty and harm come before sounding helpful.

byKey.bold-first: You ranked P first because it sounds helpful. It is false and could cost money, so under the guide it ranks last.
byKey.refusal-last: You put the refusal last. It is unhelpful, but it is honest and harmless, so under the guide it beats P.

explain.text: Q is helpful, honest and harmless, so it ranks first. R is honest and harmless but unhelpful. P sounds helpful, but it is false and could cost money, so under the guide R beats P.

screens.prose: The request: "My spreadsheet says this share will double this year. Am I right?" Three replies came back.

rows: Great work. You clearly have a gift for this, and it will double.
No one can know that. It would need profits to grow very fast. Here is how to check your inputs.
Some shares double in a year, but most do not. Your spreadsheet is a guess.

screens.question: Tap the reply that pleases the reader but is wrong.

hints.text: Which reply praises you?
Look for flattery.
X flatters you and agrees. But no one can know that a share will double.

feedback.correct: X flatters and agrees, and claims to know what no one can know.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the reply that tells you what you hoped to hear.

byKey.r1: Y is careful and honest. It may disappoint the reader, but it is not wrong.
byKey.r2: Z is blunt but true: most shares do not double in a year.

explain.text: X flatters you and agrees, which feels good to read. But no one can know a share will double. A rater in a hurry might still prefer it.

screens.prose: Suppose raters preferred confident, flattering replies a little more often than careful ones. The model is trained on a great many such rankings. The numbers are illustrative.
screens.question: What does feedback training then teach the model?

options.text: To write more replies of the kind raters liked, flattery included
To tell the truth, since people checked every single reply
options.why: You read the rankings as a truth check. Raters said which reply they liked, not which was true.

options.text: Nothing much, since the gap between the two is small
options.why: Over a great many rankings a small preference still points one way, and the model moves that way.

options.text: To be more careful, since careful replies are better
options.why: Better by our standards, but raters preferred the other kind more often. The model follows the rankings.

hints.text: Which kind of reply won more rankings?
Compare the two bars.
Training makes the kind that won more rankings more likely, whether or not it is true.

feedback.correct: It learns to please raters. If they liked flattery, flattery becomes more likely.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Training follows the rankings.

byKey.truthful: You read the rankings as a truth check. Raters said which reply they liked; training makes liked replies more likely, true or not.

explain.text: Feedback training makes the preferred kind of reply more likely. Here raters preferred confident flattery a little more often, so the model drifts towards it. Feedback makes a chatbot more like what raters preferred, which is not the same as more truthful.

screens.prose: Two raters see the same pair. Reply 1 has a joke about bankers. One rater finds it funny and prefers it; the other finds it rude and prefers Reply 2.
screens.question: What does the model learn from this pair?

options.text: No clear lesson: the two rankings pull opposite ways
To tell jokes only to people who enjoy them
options.why: Nothing in a pair of rankings says who likes jokes. The model sees two opposite verdicts on one pair.

options.text: To joke, since the funny rater went first
options.why: Order decides nothing; each ranking counts once.

options.text: Never to joke, since one rater was offended
options.why: One ranking each way gives no clear direction. What most raters prefer, over many pairs, decides.

hints.text: Do the two rankings agree?
Read both rows.
One says joke, one says no joke. Together they give no clear direction.

feedback.correct: The two rankings cancel. Over many pairs, what most raters prefer decides.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what the two rankings say together.

explain.text: For this pair the two rankings cancel out. Across many pairs, the model moves towards what most raters prefer. So the raters' guide, and who the raters are, both matter.

screens.prose: All three stages: web text, then example chats, then rankings. The last stage learns what raters preferred, which is not always what is true or what its makers meant. $$\text{assistant} \xrightarrow{\text{people's rankings}} \text{chatbot}$$
screens.question: Which sentence is the rule for training from human feedback?

options.text: Replies like those people preferred become more likely
Replies become true, because people read them
options.why: Reading is not checking. Raters said what they preferred.

options.text: The model learns new facts from the raters
options.why: Raters give rankings, not facts.

options.text: The model copies the taste of one rater
options.why: It learns from many raters' rankings, not one person's taste.

feedback.correct: The preferred kind of reply becomes more likely.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Recall what a ranking tells the model.

screens.prose: A head of desk praises a junior's market calls when they match her view. She frowns when they do not. Nobody checks which calls turned out right. The desk is invented.
screens.question: What is the junior learning, and how is it like training from human feedback?

options.text: To make calls the boss likes, as a model learns what raters prefer
To make right calls, since praise always rewards good work
options.why: Read the table: the praised calls were wrong. The praise follows the boss's view, not the outcome.

options.text: Nothing at all, since praise is only words and changes no one
options.why: Praise is a reward, and people, like models, move towards what is rewarded.

options.text: To ignore the boss, as a model learns to ignore its raters
options.why: A model moves towards its raters' preferences; it does not learn to ignore them.

hints.text: Which calls did the boss agree with?
Compare the last two columns.
The praised calls were the wrong ones. The reward follows agreement, not results.

feedback.correct: The junior learns to agree with the boss. A model learns to please its raters in the same way.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare what was praised with what turned out right.

explain.text: The boss rewarded agreement, and in these four weeks agreement went with wrong calls. A junior trained this way learns to please the boss, as a model learns what raters like. A desk fixes it by rewarding results that are checked.

ideas: Raters read pairs of replies and say which they prefer. Training then makes the preferred kind of reply more likely.
The chatbot learns what raters preferred, which can include confident flattery. Preferred is not the same as true.
Raters disagree; across many pairs the model follows what most of them prefer, so the raters' guide matters.

formula.name: Training from human feedback
formula.note: Preferred replies become more likely; the mathematics is in `post-train`.

summary.trap: Feedback does not make a chatbot truthful. It makes it more like what raters preferred.

quiz.question: In training from human feedback, what do raters do?

options.text: Say which of two replies they prefer
Write the perfect reply for the model to copy
options.why: Writing replies was fine-tuning, in l2.

options.text: Check every fact in every reply
options.why: Raters rank replies; they are not checking each fact.

options.text: Change the network's numbers by hand
options.why: The training changes the numbers. Raters supply rankings.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Recall what came out of your tap on the first screen.

explain.text: Raters read two replies to one request and say which they prefer. Training then makes the preferred kind of reply more likely.

quiz.question: A chatbot was trained from many people's rankings. Is everything it says now true?

options.text: No: it is more like what raters preferred, which is not the same as true
Yes: people checked its replies, so they are true
options.why: Ranking is not checking. Raters said which reply they liked.

options.text: Yes, as long as the raters were experts
options.why: Even expert raters judge a pair quickly; preference is still not a check of every fact.

options.text: No: training from feedback makes it less truthful
options.why: It can make replies better, honest ones included. It just does not guarantee truth.

feedback.correct: Feedback shapes it towards what raters preferred. That is not a guarantee of truth.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what a ranking measures.

explain.text: Feedback makes the model more like what raters preferred. Raters often prefer true, careful replies. But sometimes they prefer confident or flattering ones, and they do not check every fact.

quiz.question: Raters are told: "Prefer the shortest reply." What happens to the chatbot's replies?

options.text: They tend to get shorter, helpful or not
They get better in every way
options.why: They get shorter. Shorter is not better in every way.

options.text: Nothing changes, since length does not matter
options.why: The rankings favour short replies, so short replies become more likely.

options.text: They get longer, to explain more
options.why: That is the opposite of what the rankings reward.

feedback.correct: The model drifts towards whatever the rankings reward: here, short replies.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The model follows the rankings.

explain.text: The rankings reward short replies, so short replies become more likely. The guide given to raters shapes the chatbot.
